subtopic_detail: Recognising surgical urgency in an ostensibly simple cellulitis
stem:
You are the emergency department medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes admitted 12 hours ago with left leg redness and fever, treated as cellulitis with IV flucloxacillin. Overnight his pain has escalated beyond what the erythematous area would suggest and he is now systemically unwell. On examination the erythema has extended by more than a hand-breadth and the skin is dusky with a small purple bulla forming.

His leg is exquisitely tender to light touch, with pain out of proportion to the surface findings.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 98/62, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal cannula, temperature 39.1
data_table.Left leg: erythema extending from foot to mid-thigh with poorly defined margins, dusky central area, single purple bulla 2 cm, crepitus not palpable, exquisitely tender
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 22 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 108 g/L (135-175), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90), CRP 340 mg/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L
data_table.Diabetes: HbA1c 92 mmol/mol at last GP visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue IV flucloxacillin monotherapy, mark the erythematous margin with a skin pen, and reassess in 6 hours for extension before considering escalation
options.rationale: This is necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, systemic sepsis, LRINEC 10, rising creatinine). Continuing narrow-spectrum monotherapy without surgical review is fatal. Time to debridement is the primary determinant of mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.text: Escalate to IV meropenem 1 g eight-hourly plus IV clindamycin 600 mg eight-hourly plus IV vancomycin, aggressive resuscitation, and immediate surgical review for emergency debridement
options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. AU empirical antibiotic cover is IV meropenem (Gram-negative and anaerobe cover) plus IV clindamycin (anti-toxin, streptococcal Eagle effect) plus IV vancomycin (MRSA cover). Aggressive fluid resuscitation and immediate operative debridement within 6 hours reduce mortality from over 50 percent toward 20 percent. Every hour of delay increases mortality. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.text: Order urgent MRI of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before deciding on operative management to avoid unnecessary debridement in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: MRI can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but must never delay operative debridement in a septic patient with clear clinical features of nec fasc. Diagnosis is primarily clinical; surgery is diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.text: Commence hyperbaric oxygen therapy as first-line adjunctive treatment before surgical intervention to arrest tissue necrosis via oxygen delivery
options.rationale: HBO is an adjunctive therapy after adequate surgical debridement and antibiotic control, not a substitute or antecedent. Time to surgical debridement is the primary mortality determinant. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

options.text: Add IV metronidazole 500 mg eight-hourly to flucloxacillin, admit to the ward for continued observation without transfer to a surgical unit
options.rationale: Adding metronidazole to flucloxacillin does not provide adequate anti-toxin or MRSA cover, and ward-level observation without surgical debridement is inappropriate for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency with mortality 20-50 percent. Clinical features include pain out of proportion, systemic sepsis disproportionate to skin findings, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus, rapid extension, and shock. LRINEC score >=6 is suggestive (>=8 strongly suggestive) but negative LRINEC does not exclude. Empirical antibiotics: broad-spectrum beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) plus clindamycin (anti-toxin, Eagle effect against group A strep) plus vancomycin (MRSA). Aggressive fluid resuscitation.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic sepsis + dusky skin/bullae = surgical emergency
LRINEC >=6 suggestive, >=8 strongly suggestive; negative does not exclude
Meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin empirical
Emergency operative debridement within 6 hours
HBO and IVIG adjunctive; return to theatre in 24 hours for reassessment
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin adds anti-exotoxin effect against group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus (Eagle effect - beta-lactam efficacy falls at high bacterial burden), and is included even where the pathogen is likely a mixed polymicrobial synergistic infection.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic - skin and soft tissue

subtopic_detail: Sick-day hydrocortisone dosing in a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 45 year old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg at midday, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has had 24 hours of vomiting from viral gastroenteritis with inability to tolerate oral hydrocortisone. She is drowsy and cool peripherally. She reports her sick-day plan requires her to double her hydrocortisone but she could not keep the tablets down.

Her MedicAlert bracelet confirms the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, cortisol pending, ACTH pending
data_table.Perfusion: capillary refill 4 seconds, cool peripheries, dry mucosa
data_table.Established diagnosis: primary adrenal insufficiency, on stable replacement for 8 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat because it does not interfere with a subsequent short synacthen test that will confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already established (known Addison's on stable replacement); short synacthen test is not needed. Hydrocortisone is the correct replacement because it has mineralocorticoid activity at stress dose; dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and does not correct the hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.text: Give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg every 6 hours or 200 mg per 24 hours infusion, 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a known Addisonian is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg every 6 hours (or a 200 mg/24 hour infusion) with aggressive fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent saline (1 L over 30 minutes then reassess) and correction of hypoglycaemia. Hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect at stress dose so fludrocortisone is deferred until oral intake resumes. Investigate the precipitant. Diagnostic cortisol and ACTH are drawn before the first hydrocortisone dose if not already established. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.text: Give IV fludrocortisone 100 micrograms IM stat and IV normal saline; withhold hydrocortisone until oral tolerance resumes to prevent Cushingoid effects
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no parenteral form and takes days to act. Withholding hydrocortisone in a shocked Addisonian is life-threatening. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.text: Give oral hydrocortisone 40 mg dispersed in water via nasogastric tube and 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 4 hours in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: IV hydrocortisone is required in adrenal crisis - oral or NG absorption in a vomiting shocked patient is unreliable. Speed of onset with IV is critical to reversing shock. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

options.text: Commence peripheral noradrenaline infusion at 8 micrograms/min for shock and defer glucocorticoid replacement until cardiovascular stability is achieved
options.rationale: Vasopressors are ineffective in adrenal crisis without glucocorticoid replacement because vascular smooth muscle is refractory to catecholamines in cortisol deficiency. Hydrocortisone must precede or accompany any vasopressor. (Source: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg every 6 hours (or 200 mg/24 hr infusion), aggressive 0.9 percent saline fluid resuscitation, glucose correction, and search for the precipitant (infection is commonest). Hydrocortisone at stress dose has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity that fludrocortisone can be deferred until oral intake resumes. Sick-day rules for Addisonians: double the oral hydrocortisone dose for febrile illness or moderate physiological stress; hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV for vomiting/inability to take oral, then present to hospital. All patients should carry a MedicAlert, wear the bracelet, and have hydrocortisone 100 mg IM emergency ampoule at home. Prevention through education reduces mortality.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 50 mg Q6H (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)
1 L 0.9% saline stat + glucose correction
Search for precipitant (infection most common)
Sick-day rules: double oral dose; IM hydrocortisone 100 mg if unable to tolerate oral
Patient should have MedicAlert + home IM ampoule + education
explanation.pearls: Cortisone acetate 100 mg IM is the alternative if hydrocortisone unavailable; the peak cortisol level from IM cortisone is lower and slower than IM hydrocortisone but sufficient to bridge to hospital care - carry this in remote-work or extended-travel patients.

sources.label: Endocrine Society AI clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice and IV/oral switch in an admitted adult
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 38 year old woman with 24 hours of right loin pain, rigors, and dysuria for three days. She has no known drug allergy and is not pregnant. She has never had a UTI before and has no urological history. She reports one episode of vomiting on arrival.

She is systemically unwell but haemodynamically stable after 1 L of 0.9 percent saline.

data_table.Vital signs after 1 L saline: pulse 108, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Right loin: tenderness on percussion, no palpable mass
data_table.Urinalysis: leucocytes 4+, nitrites positive, blood 2+, protein trace
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 16.4 x10^9/L, CRP 148 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline unknown), lactate 2.1 mmol/L
data_table.Local antibiogram: no recent urinary Enterobacterales resistance concerns; local first-line remains gentamicin plus amoxicillin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g eight-hourly as broad-spectrum empirical cover for likely ESBL Enterobacterales in the current clinical setting under standard AU management
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum agents like piperacillin-tazobactam are reserved for severe sepsis, prior ESBL colonisation, healthcare-associated infection, or after culture-directed switch. Empirical use in a stable community-acquired pyelonephritis is unnecessary and drives resistance. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.text: IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg 12-hourly as monotherapy empirical treatment with oral switch to ciprofloxacin 500 mg 12-hourly at 48 hours to complete 7 days total
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for gram-negative resistance patterns and specific patient factors due to AU stewardship and tendonopathy/QT concerns; they are not first-line empirical treatment for pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 7 days and discharge home with GP follow-up in 48 hours in the current clinical setting under standard AU management
options.rationale: Systemic sepsis features (fever, tachycardia, raised lactate, high WCC and CRP) warrant IV therapy and admission. Oral therapy is inadequate for hospital-admitted acute pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six-hourly, with switch to oral cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate based on susceptibility in 24-48 hours to complete 10-14 days total
options.rationale: eTG recommends IV gentamicin (5 mg/kg once-daily dosing, avoid if renal impairment or age >70 or long duration) plus IV amoxicillin as empirical therapy for adult non-pregnant acute pyelonephritis in a haemodynamically stable admitted patient. Total course 10-14 days. Switch to oral once afebrile 24-48 hours, tolerating oral, guided by susceptibility (cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole per sensitivities). (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily monotherapy for 10 days without gentamicin, given the risk of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity in acute pyelonephritis in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Once-daily gentamicin at 5 mg/kg for 48 hours is safe in most patients without underlying renal impairment; concern about aminoglycoside toxicity does not override AU first-line recommendation for gentamicin plus amoxicillin. Ceftriaxone is used when aminoglycoside is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in adults presents with fever, flank pain, and lower urinary tract symptoms. Hospital admission is warranted for systemic sepsis, dehydration, inability to tolerate oral, pregnancy, or complicated urinary tract abnormality. Empirical therapy per eTG: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six-hourly, then switch to oral guided by susceptibility once afebrile and tolerating oral (typical agents cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, ciprofloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). Total duration 10-14 days for uncomplicated adult pyelonephritis. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily is the alternative if aminoglycoside contraindicated (renal impairment, elderly, prolonged duration). Ultrasound is warranted if response is slow, obstruction is suspected, or the patient is diabetic.
key_points: First-line: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg + IV amoxicillin (eTG)
Ceftriaxone if aminoglycoside contraindicated
Total duration 10-14 days
Switch oral once afebrile 24-48 h, tolerating oral, susceptibility known
Ultrasound if slow response, obstruction suspected, or diabetic
explanation.pearls: In an admitted pyelonephritis patient with slow response after 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, image urgently for obstruction, emphysematous pyelonephritis (a diabetes emergency requiring urgent urology/decompression), or perinephric abscess.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic - urinary tract infection

stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44 year old man in the endocrine outpatient clinic three weeks after admission for hypertensive crisis with headache and diaphoresis. His 24 hour urinary fractionated metanephrines returned at seven times upper limit of normal. MIBG imaging localises a 5 cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is scheduled in six weeks. He is not currently on any antihypertensive therapy.

His clinic BP today is 168/102 and he asks about starting treatment before the operation.

data_table.Vital signs today: pulse 92, blood pressure 168/102, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Investigations: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines 7x ULN, MIBG-positive right 5 cm adrenal mass
data_table.Cardiovascular: no chest pain, no cardiac history, ECG sinus rhythm, no LVH

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily titrated up over 2 weeks with liberal salt and fluid intake, then add propranolol 20 mg three times daily only after alpha-blockade is established
options.rationale: Preoperative preparation for phaeochromocytoma requires at least 10-14 days of alpha-blockade before surgery. Phenoxybenzamine (non-competitive, irreversible) is traditional; doxazosin (selective alpha-1) is an alternative and widely used in Australia. Beta-blockade is ADDED after alpha-blockade is established (target orthostatic hypotension, mild nasal congestion) to avoid unopposed alpha-agonism which precipitates hypertensive crisis. Liberal salt and fluid intake reverses catecholamine-induced volume contraction. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline

options.text: Commence oral atenolol 50 mg daily as first-line therapy to control the tachycardia and hypertension, then add doxazosin 4 mg daily one week before surgery
options.rationale: Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade precipitates severe hypertensive crisis by unopposed alpha stimulation (loss of beta-2 mediated vasodilation). This is a fatal sequencing error. Alpha always precedes beta. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline

options.text: Commence oral amlodipine 5 mg daily and no other antihypertensive, deferring alpha and beta blockade until the day before surgery to avoid symptomatic hypotension
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line adjuncts to alpha-blockade, not substitutes. Deferring alpha-blockade until day-before surgery does not allow time to establish volume expansion and receptor blockade, and intraoperative haemodynamic swings become extreme and dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline

options.text: Commence oral perindopril 5 mg daily and salt restriction as standard hypertension management until surgical review in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are not the primary agents for phaeochromocytoma-related hypertension. Salt restriction worsens intravascular volume contraction. This management strategy is inadequate and dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline

options.text: Commence oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily as combined alpha and beta blockade in a single agent to simplify preoperative preparation in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Labetalol has beta blockade activity greater than alpha (roughly 7:1 ratio when oral), so it delivers de facto beta-first blockade and is not an accepted preoperative regimen for phaeochromocytoma. Sequential alpha-then-beta with dedicated agents is the standard. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma guideline

explanation.summary: Preoperative preparation of phaeochromocytoma is critical to prevent intraoperative catecholamine-triggered hypertensive crisis and postoperative refractory hypotension. Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine 10-20 mg twice daily titrated up, or doxazosin 4-16 mg daily as the AU preferred option in many centres) is initiated at least 10-14 days before surgery, with target orthostatic hypotension, mild nasal congestion, and BP <130/80 seated with SBP >90 standing. Liberal salt and fluid intake reverses catecholamine-induced volume contraction (usually 5 g salt/day plus 2-3 L fluid). Beta-blockade (propranolol, atenolol) is added ONLY after alpha-blockade is established, to control catecholamine-induced tachycardia; beta-before-alpha causes hypertensive crisis by unopposed alpha stimulation. Calcium channel blockers or metyrosine may be adjuncts. Intraoperative hypotension after tumour removal is managed with fluids and vasopressors.
key_points: Alpha-blockade at least 10-14 days before surgery
Phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin (AU preferred selective alpha-1)
Beta-blockade added AFTER alpha-blockade is established
Liberal salt and fluid intake (5 g NaCl + 2-3 L fluid) - reverses catecholamine volume contraction
Beta-first causes hypertensive crisis (unopposed alpha)
explanation.pearls: Metyrosine (tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor) blocks catecholamine synthesis and is added for particularly biochemically active tumours or before surgery for metastatic disease when receptor blockade alone is insufficient - specialist endocrine referral required.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between IVIG and plasmapheresis in a rapidly deteriorating patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 52 year old woman with a two-year history of myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg five times daily and prednisolone 20 mg daily. She presented 12 hours ago with rapid worsening bulbar and respiratory weakness after starting azithromycin two days earlier for a chest infection. Her vital capacity has fallen from an admission 2.1 L to 1.2 L over the last four hours. Negative inspiratory pressure is now -20 cmH2O.

She has not previously required plasmapheresis or IVIG.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 26 shallow, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4
data_table.Bulbar: dysarthria worsening, weak cough, drooling of saliva, unable to swallow reliably
data_table.Respiratory function: vital capacity 1.2 L (baseline 3.4 L; alarm threshold usually <15 mL/kg or 1 L; NIP -20 cmH2O with -30 as threshold)
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): white cells 12 x10^9/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, IgA level pending
data_table.Chest X-ray: right lower lobe consolidation being treated
data_table.Precipitant: azithromycin recently commenced (aminoglycoside/macrolide class known to worsen myasthenia)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit to intensive care, cease azithromycin, prepare for intubation given falling vital capacity, start intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days
options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis is defined by respiratory or bulbar failure requiring intensive care admission and often ventilatory support. Vital capacity below 20 mL/kg (about 1.4 L in a 70 kg patient) or NIP less negative than -30 cmH2O warrants preparation for intubation. IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days is equivalent to plasmapheresis in efficacy (large trials show non-inferiority) but IVIG is more available, does not require specialised access, and is often the first-line AU choice. Removing the precipitant (azithromycin worsens myasthenia via presynaptic effect) is critical. Continue steroids because sudden withdrawal precipitates crisis. Pyridostigmine may need dose adjustment. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)
source_refs: RACP myasthenia gravis

options.text: Double the pyridostigmine dose to 120 mg every 4 hours to maximise cholinergic transmission before deciding on advanced therapies
options.rationale: Escalating pyridostigmine in crisis risks cholinergic crisis (indistinguishable from myasthenic crisis except by edrophonium test) and increases secretions worsening respiratory function. In severe crisis pyridostigmine is often reduced or withheld. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)
source_refs: RACP myasthenia gravis

options.text: Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days as high-dose pulse steroid therapy and defer IVIG or plasmapheresis to see if steroid response occurs first
options.rationale: High-dose steroids can transiently WORSEN myasthenic weakness before improvement (10-day worsening window). In active respiratory failure a rapid-acting immunotherapy (IVIG or plasmapheresis) is needed, not pulse steroid alone. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)
source_refs: RACP myasthenia gravis

options.text: Give a single IV dose of edrophonium 10 mg to differentiate cholinergic crisis from myasthenic crisis before further therapy
options.rationale: Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing carries significant risks (bradycardia, bronchospasm) and is largely superseded. Diagnosis rests on clinical picture, medication review and serial vital capacity. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)
source_refs: RACP myasthenia gravis

options.text: Administer intramuscular neostigmine 1.5 mg six-hourly as an alternative to pyridostigmine while awaiting immunotherapy
options.rationale: Neostigmine has a shorter half-life and greater muscarinic effects than pyridostigmine and does not address the underlying immune process. Switching cholinesterase inhibitors is not disease-modifying. (Source: RACP myasthenia gravis)
source_refs: RACP myasthenia gravis

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is bulbar and/or respiratory failure requiring intensive care. Common precipitants: infection, aspiration, non-compliance, medications (macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers, high-dose IV corticosteroid). Assess respiratory function with vital capacity and NIP - VC <20 mL/kg (about 1 L in a 60 kg patient) or NIP less negative than -30 cmH2O warrants preparation for intubation. IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and plasmapheresis (5-7 sessions) are equally effective; IVIG is often first-line in AU practice due to availability. Continue steroid to prevent adrenal crisis; pyridostigmine may be reduced. Immunomodulation with mycophenolate, azathioprine, or rituximab is planned for the outpatient long term. Precipitant removal (drug, infection treatment) is essential.
key_points: Crisis = respiratory/bulbar failure needing ICU
VC <20 mL/kg or NIP > -30 = prepare to intubate
IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days ~ plasmapheresis; IVIG usually AU first-line
Remove precipitant (macrolides, aminoglycosides, magnesium)
Continue steroid; pyridostigmine may be reduced in crisis
explanation.pearls: In seronegative myasthenia gravis (no anti-AChR antibody) check for anti-MuSK antibodies which are more common in women and often more bulbar-predominant with less pyridostigmine response - rituximab is particularly effective for MuSK-positive disease.

subtopic_detail: Stanford classification and immediate management divergence
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 62 year old man with sudden onset tearing interscapular chest pain radiating to the back that woke him from sleep 90 minutes ago. He has a background of hypertension on irbesartan and smokes 30 pack years. A CT aortogram has just returned and shows a dissection flap starting at the ascending aorta and extending distally through the arch and descending thoracic aorta to the level of the diaphragm. There is no pericardial effusion or ischaemic complication.

He has a mild new murmur of aortic regurgitation and his left brachial pulse is diminished compared with the right.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 168/98 (left arm 142/86), respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L nasal cannula, temperature 36.9
data_table.CT aortogram: dissection flap ascending aorta through arch and descending thoracic aorta to diaphragm; no pericardial effusion; no coronary involvement; no visceral ischaemia; false lumen patent
data_table.Cardiovascular: new soft early diastolic murmur, left brachial pulse diminished, no tamponade
data_table.Bloods: troponin negative, D-dimer elevated, creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit to the coronary care unit for medical management with IV labetalol only, and interval outpatient thoracic surgery review in 4 weeks given absence of pericardial effusion
options.rationale: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency regardless of complications - ascending aorta involvement carries prohibitive medical-management mortality within hours. Delaying surgery for outpatient review is fatal. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)
source_refs: eTG Complete Cardiology

options.text: IV nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg as initial management, without prior beta-blockade to allow for rapid titration
options.rationale: Vasodilators alone (nitroprusside, GTN) cause reflex tachycardia which increases aortic wall shear stress (dP/dt) and worsens dissection propagation. Beta-blockade must precede any vasodilator therapy. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)
source_refs: eTG Complete Cardiology

options.text: IV heparin infusion for suspected pulmonary embolism given the pleuritic chest pain and mediastinal widening on chest radiograph in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: Heparin in acute aortic dissection worsens haemorrhage and is contraindicated. CT aortogram has confirmed dissection - PE is not the diagnosis and empirical anticoagulation is harmful. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)
source_refs: eTG Complete Cardiology

options.text: IV labetalol infusion titrated to target heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, IV opioid analgesia, and immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral for open aortic repair
options.rationale: This is Stanford Type A dissection (ascending aorta involved). It is a surgical emergency with mortality of 1-2 percent per hour without operative repair. Management: aggressive impulse control with IV beta-blockade to target HR 60-80 and SBP 100-120 (labetalol infusion, or esmolol; add IV GTN if further BP control needed after HR is controlled - never before), analgesia (IV morphine), and immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral. Type B (descending only) is managed medically unless malperfusion or rupture. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology / RACS aortic dissection)
source_refs: eTG Complete Cardiology

options.text: Endovascular thoracic aortic stenting via femoral access as first-line intervention for a dissection extending into the descending aorta in the current clinical setting
options.rationale: TEVAR is the definitive intervention for complicated Type B dissections (malperfusion, rupture, uncontrolled pain). Type A dissections require open surgical repair; endovascular stenting of the ascending aorta is not standard first-line. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiology)
source_refs: eTG Complete Cardiology

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection: Stanford A involves the ascending aorta (~60 percent, surgical emergency, untreated mortality 1-2 percent per hour); Stanford B is distal to the left subclavian only (~40 percent, medical management with impulse control unless complicated). Initial management is aggressive impulse control: IV beta-blockade first (labetalol, esmolol, metoprolol) to HR 60-80 and SBP 100-120, then IV vasodilator (GTN, nitroprusside) if further BP control needed. Beta-blockade must precede vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia. Analgesia and cardiothoracic surgical referral for Type A. For Type B, TEVAR is indicated for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension. Long-term BP control, aggressive risk factor reduction, and imaging surveillance are lifelong.
key_points: Type A = ascending aorta = surgical emergency (~2%/hr untreated mortality)
Type B = distal only = medical management unless complicated (TEVAR)
Impulse control: beta-blockade FIRST to HR 60-80, SBP 100-120
Vasodilator (GTN, nitroprusside) added AFTER beta-blockade if needed
Anticoagulation contraindicated; opioid analgesia; urgent cardiothoracic referral
explanation.pearls: In dissection with new aortic regurgitation murmur or pericardial effusion, do not perform pericardiocentesis unless in extremis - decompressing the tamponade removes the tamponade effect that is limiting further bleeding into the pericardium and precipitates death from exsanguination into the pericardial sac.
